content.title: About
content.content: Artichoke dip is a creamy appetizer made from cooked artichoke hearts, cream cheese, mayonnaise, and seasonings. It has a mild, slightly nutty flavor and a smooth texture, perfect for serving with crackers, vegetable sticks, or as a spread for sandwiches.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Artichokes have been cultivated in the Mediterranean for over 2,000 years.
The modern American artichoke dip emerged in the 1950s when cream cheese was added to the classic recipe.
Artichokes are rich in antioxidants, especially cynarin, which helps protect cells from oxidative stress.
Traditional recipes use only the tender heart of the artichoke.
The dip is a popular party appetizer for holidays such as Thanksgiving and Christmas.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Artichokes contain cynarin and quercetin, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber in artichokes promotes healthy bowel movements and gut flora.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Low in sugar
items.content: The dip fits well into low‑carb diets when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cream cheese and mayonnaise can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Because of the cheese and mayo, the dip is calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Store‑bought versions may contain a lot of salt, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Some people experience gas or discomfort after eating artichokes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve artichoke dip chilled with crackers, pita chips, fresh vegetable sticks, or use as a sandwich spread. It can also be folded into casseroles or pasta for extra creaminess.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dip in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5‑7 days. For longer storage, freeze in small portions for up to 2 months. Bring to room temperature before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Grape Juice is a 100 % natural fruit juice specially formulated for children from 1 year old. The juice is pasteurized and contains no added sugar, colourings or preservatives. It is rich in B‑vitamins, vitamin C and antioxidants that support healthy development.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Grape juice contains natural polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.
Baby Toddler juice undergoes double pasteurization to ensure microbiological safety.
The product is packaged in convenient 200 ml cartons, ideal for on‑the‑go toddler meals.
Grapes used for the juice are grown without genetically modified organisms.
The mild sweet taste is usually well accepted by children without the need for added sugar.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Supports the immune system and aids iron absorption from plant foods.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Play a role in energy metabolism and nervous system development.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Help protect cells from free radicals, important for growth and development.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Provides additional fluid to help maintain proper hydration in toddlers.

items.title: Easy digestibility
items.content: Pasteurized juice is gentle on a young stomach and unlikely to cause digestive upset.

items.title: Grape allergy
items.content: Some children may be allergic to grapes; discontinue use at the first sign of a reaction.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although no sugar is added, natural sugars are present; moderation is recommended to avoid excess sugar intake.

items.title: Not for infants under 1 year
items.content: Due to the risk of botulism and an immature digestive system, the juice should be introduced only after the first birthday.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the juice chilled in small portions (30–50 ml) right after a meal or as a snack. It pairs well with fruit purees or yogurt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the carton in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, refrigerate and consume within 3‑5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Butter, NFS (4912) is a plain unsalted butter made from pasteurized cow's milk. It has a mild creamy flavor, smooth texture, and a light‑yellow color. Suitable for cooking, baking, and as a spread.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Butter typically contains about 80 % fat, 15 % water, and a small amount of protein.
The NFS (No Further Specification) label indicates the product meets basic standards without added flavors or colorants.
Traditional butter was churned by hand; modern production is fully automated.
Butter can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 3 months and in the freezer for up to 12 months.
Different countries have regulations on salt content; Butter, NFS contains no added salt.

items.title: Source of fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Butter provides vitamins A, D, E, and K, which support vision, immunity, and blood clotting.

items.title: Contains conjugated linoleic acid (CLA)
items.content: CLA may help maintain a healthy weight and improve insulin sensitivity.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: The fats in butter are readily absorbed, providing sustained satiety.

items.title: Supports skin health
items.content: Vitamin A and fatty acids aid in skin barrier repair.

items.title: Contains biotin
items.content: Biotin is important for the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: Excessive intake may raise LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Butter contains trace amounts of lactose, which can cause discomfort for sensitive individuals.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some people may react to casein present in butter.

items.title: Fat oxidation
items.content: When stored at high temperatures for long periods, butter can become rancid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Butter, NFS can be spread on bread, used in sauces, for sautéing, and in baking cookies, cakes, and pastries. For optimal flavor, let the butter sit at room temperature for about 30 minutes before use.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store butter in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at +2‑+6 °C. For long‑term storage, freeze up to 12 months, preferably divided into portions.

chicken-leg-drumstick-and-thigh-rotisser.title: Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh, rotisserie, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken legs, drumsticks and thighs prepared on a rotisserie are juicy pieces of meat with a crispy skin. The rotating heat ensures even cooking and a golden, aromatic crust. This product is popular in fast‑food outlets, as a snack, and in home meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark‑meat chicken parts contain more fat than breast meat, making them more flavorful.
Rotisserie cooking creates a uniform crust thanks to constant rotation and circulating hot air.
Leaving the skin on helps retain moisture inside the meat and adds a smoky aroma.
In many countries the rotisserie chicken legs are sold pre‑cooked and only need reheating.
Chicken thighs are a staple in traditional dishes such as paprika stew or braised drumsticks.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken legs and thighs provide high‑quality complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Dark meat supplies more iron than white meat, supporting healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is important for nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Provides zinc
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Contains collagen
items.content: Skin and connective tissue in chicken are rich in collagen, beneficial for skin and joint health.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Legs and thighs are fattier than breast meat, so moderation is advised for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Improper cooking can lead to salmonella; ensure internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium in prepared products
items.content: Pre‑seasoned rotisserie chicken often contains added salt; people with hypertension should watch intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken legs, drumsticks and thighs can be eaten hot, sliced into bite‑size pieces, or added to salads, sandwiches and rice dishes. The skin can be enjoyed as a crunchy snack or removed for a leaner option. They pair well with barbecue, mustard or creamy sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked pieces in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage freeze in a bag at –18 °C for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide. This entry describes a piece of chicken breast grilled without sauce, with the skin left on and edible. Grilling preserves the natural flavor while adding a smoky aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken meat is a complete source of all essential amino acids.
Grilling creates a distinctive flavor through Maillard reactions.
Chicken is one of the most affordable animal protein sources globally.
The skin contains more fat than the breast meat but also provides beneficial monounsaturated fats.
Culinary traditions around the world feature chicken in countless ways, from simple grills to complex marinades.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100 g serving of chicken breast provides about 31 g of high‑quality protein, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Chicken contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6), which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides phosphorus, selenium, and zinc—nutrients essential for bone health, immune function, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Beneficial fats in the skin
items.content: When eaten in moderation, chicken skin adds monounsaturated fatty acids that can support heart health.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter. Cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F).

items.title: High sodium in marinades
items.content: If the meat was pre‑marinated, watch the salt content to avoid excessive sodium intake.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: A small number of people are allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Fatty skin
items.content: Chicken skin increases the calorie density of the dish and should be consumed in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Grilled chicken breast can be served as a main dish, sliced into salads, added to sandwiches, or used in Asian‑style stir‑fries. The skin can be eaten together with the meat or removed according to personal preference.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked chicken in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag at –18 °C, where it keeps quality for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: A reduced‑fat chocolate sandwich cookie. Crispy baked wafers are filled with a smooth chocolate cream, offering a light snack with fewer calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sandwich cookie originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a convenient snack for children.
Reduced fat is achieved by replacing part of the butter with plant oils and using aeration techniques during baking.
The chocolate filling contains cocoa mass but no extra added sugars, preserving the classic taste.
The product is often included in school lunch programs because of its handy packaging and moderate energy content.

items.title: Lower calorie content
items.content: Reduced fat lowers the overall calorie count, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: The cookie provides quick‑release complex carbohydrates, useful for active individuals.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Cocoa in the chocolate cream supplies non‑heme iron, supporting normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Plant‑based oils
items.content: The oils used are rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids, beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The cookie contains wheat flour, which may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Despite reduced fat, the product still contains sugar, so portion control is advised for diabetics.

items.title: Caffeine in cocoa
items.content: The chocolate cream may contain small amounts of caffeine, which should be considered for children and caffeine‑sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookie as a stand‑alone snack, in school lunchboxes, or paired with fruit and yogurt. A brief microwave warm‑up can soften the chocolate filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place, in the original package or an airtight container. At temperatures above 25 °C the cookie may soften and the chocolate cream may discolor.

content.title: About
content.content: Eggplant (Solanum melongena), also called aubergine, is a glossy, deep purple (or white, green, or striped) vegetable with spongy flesh, native to India and Southeast Asia. It has a mild, slightly bitter flavor and absorbs the flavors of the dishes it is cooked in. Eggplant is eaten cooked, roasted, grilled, fried, stuffed, or pureed.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Botanically, eggplant is a fruit, classified as a berry, and belongs to the nightshade family with tomatoes and potatoes.
Eggplants come in many shapes and colors, including long, round, white, green, and striped varieties.
Its spongy flesh absorbs oil and flavors readily.
Salting cut eggplant before cooking can reduce bitterness and the amount of oil it absorbs.
Eggplant is a staple in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, Indian, and Asian cuisines.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Eggplant contributes fiber that supports digestion and fullness.

items.title: Contains anthocyanins
items.content: The purple skin contains nasunin, an anthocyanin with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Contains manganese and potassium
items.content: These minerals support normal metabolism and blood pressure.

items.title: Provides vitamin K and vitamin C
items.content: These vitamins support blood clotting and the immune system.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Eggplant is low in calories, though it absorbs a lot of oil when fried.

items.title: Nightshade sensitivity
items.content: Eggplant belongs to the nightshade family, and some people report sensitivity or allergy to these vegetables.

items.title: Raw eggplant
items.content: Raw eggplant is bitter and can cause stomach upset, so cook it thoroughly.

items.title: Oil absorption
items.content: Frying eggplant makes it absorb a lot of oil and calories, so baking, roasting, or grilling is a lighter option.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Eggplant contains some oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eggplant can be roasted, grilled, baked, stir-fried, steamed, stuffed, or made into dishes such as baba ganoush, ratatouille, moussaka, and curries. Slice and salt it before cooking if you want to reduce bitterness, then rinse and pat dry. Cook until soft and creamy inside.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store eggplant in a cool place or in the refrigerator crisper drawer and use it within a few days to a week, since it is sensitive to both cold and heat. Keep it whole until cooking, because cut eggplant browns quickly. Cooked eggplant should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to five days.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate milk shake is a beverage made from milk, ice cream or frozen yogurt, cocoa powder or melted chocolate, and sometimes add‑ins like banana, nuts or spices. It has a thick, creamy texture and a rich chocolate flavor, perfect as a dessert snack or post‑workout energy boost.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chocolate milk shakes became popular in the United States in the 1950s when ice cream started being blended into drinks.
A classic recipe uses 250 ml milk, 2 tablespoons ice cream, and 2 teaspoons cocoa powder.
A pinch of salt enhances the perception of sweetness and chocolate depth.
In many countries the shake is topped with whipped cream and chocolate shavings.
Homemade versions let you control sugar levels and add healthy boosters such as protein powder.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Milk, the main base, is rich in calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Protein rich
items.content: Adding protein powder or yogurt turns the shake into a high‑quality protein source.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: Combined carbs from sugar and fats from ice cream rapidly replenish energy stores.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa powder is high in flavonoids, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Mood enhancer
items.content: Chocolate stimulates serotonin and endorphin production, improving mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Traditional recipes contain a lot of sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and raise blood glucose.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance should use lactose‑free milk or plant‑based alternatives.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Allergy to cow’s milk requires substitution with dairy‑free options.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The creamy texture from ice cream makes the shake calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Ice cream and cream can contain saturated fats, which in excess may affect cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the shake cold, immediately after blending, in tall glasses. Top with whipped cream, chocolate shavings or sprinkles if desired. For a lighter version, replace ice cream with frozen yogurt or banana.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The shake is best enjoyed right away. If needed, store it in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Shake well before serving as ingredients may separate.

content.title: About
content.content: A peanut butter sandwich is made with white bread spread with reduced‑fat peanut butter. It is a quick, easy snack that provides energy from carbohydrates and plant‑based protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Reduced‑fat peanut butter typically contains about 30 % fat instead of 50 % in regular versions.
White bread is often used in children’s meals because of its soft texture and neutral flavor.
Peanut butter sandwiches have been popular in the United States for over a century.
Peanuts are legumes, not true nuts, so they do not contain the same allergen profile as tree nuts.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peanut butter provides roughly 8 g of protein per 2 tbsp, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Contains heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Even with reduced fat, it retains monounsaturated fats that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Provides magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals aid normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides quick energy
items.content: Carbohydrates from white bread are rapidly absorbed, giving an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanuts are a strong allergen; individuals with a peanut allergy may experience severe reactions.

items.title: High glycemic index of white bread
items.content: White bread can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar, which may be undesirable for people with diabetes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some reduced‑fat peanut butter products add salt; choose unsalted versions when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread 1–2 tbsp of reduced‑fat peanut butter on two slices of white bread, press them together, and optionally cut the sandwich in half. For extra flavor, add banana slices or a drizzle of honey.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich in an airtight container at room temperature for no more than 4 hours. Store opened peanut butter in the refrigerator and keep bread in a dry place.

potato-baked-peel-not-eaten-with-vegetab.title: Potato, baked, peel not eaten, with vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Baked potato is a tuber that has been roasted in the oven until a golden crust forms. The peel is not consumed, and the dish is served with a variety of vegetables such as carrots, broccoli, bell pepper, and onion.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potato is the fourth most consumed food worldwide after rice, wheat, and corn.
Baking retains more B‑vitamins and minerals compared with frying.
The potato skin contains more fiber and antioxidants, but it is omitted in this preparation.
Combining potato with vegetables boosts vitamin C and dietary fiber content.
Baked potato is easily digestible and suitable for moderate‑glycemic diets.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: Potato provides a slow‑release source of energy, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium supports fluid balance and heart function.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C enhances immunity and participates in collagen synthesis.

items.title: Dietary fiber from vegetables
items.content: The added vegetables increase fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Baking without excessive oil makes the dish light.

items.title: Solanine in the peel
items.content: The potato skin can contain the toxic compound solanine, so it is best not to eat it.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to potato.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Large portions can raise blood sugar quickly.

items.title: Nitrate content in vegetables
items.content: Certain vegetables may contain nitrates; choose fresh produce and wash thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut the baked potato into pieces, add steamed or boiled vegetables, drizzle with olive oil, season with salt and herbs. Serve warm as a side dish or a main course.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave before serving.

potato-mashed-from-fresh-made-with-milk-.title: Mashed Potatoes with Milk and Gravy

content.title: About
content.content: Mashed potatoes made from fresh potatoes, prepared with milk and gravy, are a smooth, creamy side dish. The potatoes are boiled until tender, then mashed with milk for a silky texture, while the gravy adds a flavorful, slightly thick sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes are one of the world’s most consumed root vegetables; in 2020 global production exceeded 370 million tonnes.
The tradition of making mashed potatoes with milk began in Europe in the 19th century when milk became more widely available.
Gravy for mashed potatoes is often made from meat stock, but vegetarian versions using vegetable broth are common.
Mashed potatoes are a classic accompaniment to roasted meat, fish, and poultry.
There are many variations: with butter, cheese, garlic, or herbs.

items.title: Rich source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes provide potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C content
items.content: Fresh potatoes contain vitamin C, which helps boost immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates for energy
items.content: The carbs in mashed potatoes supply sustained energy.

items.title: Calcium from milk
items.content: Milk adds calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Low fat when made with skim milk
items.content: Using low‑fat milk keeps the dish relatively low in calories.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or milk allergy may experience reactions.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes can raise blood sugar quickly, so those with diabetes should watch portion size.

items.title: Sodium in gravy
items.content: Prepared gravies can be salty; low‑sodium versions are recommended.

items.title: Bacterial growth if improperly stored
items.content: Leaving mashed potatoes at room temperature for long periods can promote bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the mash hot as a side to meat, fish, or vegetable dishes. Top with fried onions, fresh herbs, grated cheese, or a pat of butter. For a lighter version, use skim milk and reduce the amount of gravy.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the mash to room temperature, then place it in an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 3 days. When reheating, add a splash of milk to restore creaminess. It can be frozen for up to 2 months, though texture may become slightly grainy.

content.title: About
content.content: A tuna cake (or patty) is a ready‑to‑eat product made from whole tuna fillet mixed with a small amount of breadcrumbs, eggs and seasonings, shaped into a round patty and pre‑cooked by pan‑frying or baking. It has a delicate sea flavor, firm texture and can be served on its own or used in salads, sandwiches and burgers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna is one of the most protein‑rich and omega‑3‑rich fish species.
Tuna patties are often used in Japanese cuisine as “tuna‑patti” for sushi rolls.
A touch of starch or breadcrumbs is added during production to help the patty hold its shape.
The patty retains most of the nutrients of fresh tuna thanks to a short heat treatment.
In some countries the product is sold frozen in individual portions for quick preparation.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Tuna cake provides about 20‑25 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: EPA and DHA support heart and brain health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with red meat, tuna patty contains less saturated fat, making it a leaner choice.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rich in B12, niacin and B6, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Contains selenium, iodine and phosphorus, which aid immunity and thyroid function.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: People allergic to seafood may experience reactions to tuna.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Tuna can contain trace amounts of mercury; intake should be limited for children and pregnant women.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Some ready‑made patties contain added salt; check the label if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Industrial versions may include preservatives; choose additive‑free options if preferred.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the tuna patty in a skillet, oven or microwave and serve with vegetable sides, in a bun, in a salad, or thinly sliced for sushi rolls. It pairs well with soy sauce, lemon, mustard and fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage freeze in an airtight bag at ‑18 °C for up to 2 months. Thaw completely before use and discard if it develops an off‑odor.
